passage:
Home-visit notes, community nurse, Thursday.
Visited Mr Dave, bedridden since spring. His daughter Hansa has been the main carer. Last month she looked grey with tiredness and said she hadn't slept a full night in weeks. Today there was a change. Her son Jagdish, who works in the city, has made a chart on the fridge: who does night turns, who cooks, who handles medicines, with his sister and a cousin on it too. He asked me directly whether Hansa was eating properly and whether the bathroom was safe for her at night. He admitted he had skipped his own badminton for a month and was getting snappy. We agreed he would keep Wednesday evenings for himself.
What I did next: I gave the family the number of the carers' support group, and booked a doctor's check-up for Hansa next week.

qa.q: What did Jagdish put on the fridge?
qa.a: A chart: who does night turns, who cooks, who handles medicines.

qa.q: How had Hansa been feeling last month, and what showed it?
qa.a: Exhausted; she looked grey with tiredness and said she hadn't slept a full night in weeks.

qa.q: Why was keeping Wednesday evenings for himself a wise choice for Jagdish?
qa.a: He had skipped badminton and was getting snappy; protecting some time for himself guards against burnout so he can keep helping.

qa.q: How might Hansa feel seeing her son's chart and questions?
qa.a: She may feel relieved and cared for, no longer carrying every night turn alone.

grounding: It shows a son checking his caregiving mother's sleep, meals and safety, sharing tasks, bringing in professional help and protecting his own time.

passage:
Saturday night.
Came home at seven and found Ma asleep sitting up beside Thakuma's bed, the dinner pot still cold on the stove. I realised I couldn't remember the last time I'd seen her eat lunch. She keeps saying, "Thakuma needs me, I'm fine," but she's snapping at everyone and forgetting her own headache tablets.
So tonight I did three things. I heated the dal and sat with her until she'd eaten it. I called Mashi and asked her to take Sundays with Thakuma; she said yes straight away, sounding almost relieved to be asked. And I booked Ma an appointment with Dr Sen for Tuesday, for the headaches and the tiredness.
I also nearly cancelled my trek with Charu next month. Then I pictured both Ma and me burnt out. I'm keeping it.
Bidisha

qa.q: What did Bidisha find when coming home at seven?
qa.a: Ma asleep sitting up beside Thakuma's bed, the dinner pot still cold on the stove.

qa.q: What worried Bidisha about Ma?
qa.a: Bidisha was worried because Ma was sleeping sitting up, skipping lunch, snapping at everyone and forgetting her own tablets.

qa.q: Why was keeping the trek with Charu a wise choice?
qa.a: Bidisha saw that giving up everything would lead to both Ma and Bidisha burning out, which would help nobody.

qa.q: How might Mashi see being asked to take Sundays?
qa.a: She sounded almost relieved, perhaps glad to be allowed to help instead of watching from the side.

grounding: It shows a young adult checking Ma's meals, sleep and health while Ma cares for Thakuma, sharing tasks with Mashi, booking a doctor and protecting their own life.

passage:
Vikas: Ma sounded so tired on the phone. Since Papa's stroke she's doing everything alone
Tenzin: is she sleeping?
Vikas: she says 4 hours. she eats standing up
Tenzin: that can't go on. she'll burn out
Vikas: I feel guilty I'm not there all the time
Tenzin: you can't be. but we can plan
Tenzin: what if you take weekends, and your cousin covers Wednesdays?
Vikas: and I'll ask Papa's doctor about a home nurse and a counsellor for Ma
Tenzin: yes. and you keep your Thursday badminton. you need it too
Vikas: feels selfish
Tenzin: it isn't. if you burn out, who helps her then?
Vikas: ok. calling Ma now to check she's eaten

qa.q: How many hours does Ma say she sleeps?
qa.a: Four hours.

qa.q: How does Vikas feel about not being there all the time?
qa.a: Vikas feels guilty, and even a little selfish about keeping badminton.

qa.q: What makes the plan wise?
qa.a: It checks on Ma's sleep and meals, shares tasks with a cousin, seeks a home nurse and counsellor, and protects Vikas's own time.

qa.q: How might Tenzin see Vikas's badminton?
qa.a: Tenzin sees it as necessary self-care, not selfishness, because burnout would help nobody.

grounding: Shows a family member checking on a caregiving parent's sleep and meals, sharing tasks, seeking professional help and protecting their own life to avoid burnout.

passage: Avni, twenty-five, came home to the village for the weekend and found her mother, Manjula, asleep sitting up beside Dadi's bed at noon. Dadi now forgot names and wandered at night. Ma had grown thin and snappish. Avni checked the kitchen: no proper meal cooked in days. That evening she made rice and dal, sat Ma down and made sure she ate. "Ma, you can't do nights alone any more." She called her cousin Sunita, who agreed to stay two nights a week. She walked to the health centre and asked the doctor about help for Dadi and for Ma's exhaustion. On Monday morning Avni took the bus back to her job. "I'll call every evening, and come every second weekend," she promised. Ma hugged her hard.

qa.q: What did Avni cook for her mother?
qa.a: Rice and dal.

qa.q: How did Avni feel seeing her mother asleep sitting up at noon?
qa.a: She felt worried and concerned, seeing how exhausted Ma had become.

qa.q: What did Avni do that cared for the caregiver wisely?
qa.a: She made sure Ma ate, arranged her cousin to share nights, sought the health centre doctor's help and kept her own job with regular check-ins.

qa.q: How might Manjula feel when Avni leaves on Monday?
qa.a: Manjula may feel supported and less alone, knowing help is arranged and Avni will call every evening.

grounding: Shows a family member checking a caregiving parent's sleep and meals, sharing tasks, seeking professional help and protecting her own life to avoid burnout.

passage: In Lagos, Nkechi, twenty-six, noticed her father looked grey with tiredness. Since her mother's hip surgery, he had done everything: cooking, lifting, medicines at midnight. He said he was fine, but he'd lost his appetite and dozed at the table. Nkechi talked to her brother Omar. "We check on him, not just on Mum." They made a rota: Omar took mornings, Nkechi evenings. She asked the hospital social worker about a home nurse for two afternoons a week, and got Dad to see his own doctor about his sleep. And she didn't cancel her Saturday football. "If I collapse too, Dad has two patients," she told Omar. On Sunday, her father slept till nine for the first time in a month.

qa.q: Who is Nkechi's brother?
qa.a: Omar.

qa.q: How did Nkechi feel noticing her father's tiredness?
qa.a: She felt worried and protective, seeing he was grey, not eating and dozing.

qa.q: What steps did Nkechi and Omar take to care for their father?
qa.a: They made a rota, got help from the hospital social worker for a home nurse, took Dad to his doctor and Nkechi protected her own time.

qa.q: How might Nkechi's father feel after sleeping till nine?
qa.a: He likely feels rested and relieved that the load is finally shared.

grounding: Shows adult children checking on a caregiving parent's sleep and meals, sharing tasks, seeking professional help and protecting their own lives.

passage:
The visitors' room at the Ernakulam day-care centre for older people was quiet at four. Binita watched her father, Thomas, sign out Ammachi, his hands trembling. For two years he had cared for his mother alone since her memory began to fail.
"Pappa, when did you last sleep a full night?" Binita asked.
He laughed tiredly. "What is full?"
"Have you eaten today?"
"Tea."
Binita took the bag from him. She'd been noticing for weeks. That evening she made a list. She would take Ammachi on Tuesdays and Saturdays. Her brother would pay for a night helper twice a week. She asked the centre's social worker about a caregivers' support group and booked Pappa a check-up with his own doctor.
But she kept her Thursday evenings for her dance class. "If I burn out, Pappa, we both fall," she told him. He nodded, and for the first time didn't argue.

qa.q: Which evenings did Binita keep for herself?
qa.a: Her Thursday evenings, for her dance class.

qa.q: How was Thomas feeling after two years of caring alone?
qa.a: He felt exhausted and worn down, not sleeping properly and barely eating, with trembling hands.

qa.q: What did Binita get right as a family member helping the caregiver?
qa.a: She checked his sleep and meals, shared tasks with her brother, sought professional support and a check-up, and protected her own life to avoid burnout.

qa.q: How might Ammachi's days change with Binita's plan?
qa.a: She would still be cared for, but by a less exhausted son and a wider circle, which may make her days calmer and safer.

grounding: Binita checks her caregiver father's sleep, meals and health, shares tasks, seeks professional support and protects her own life to avoid burnout.
